statement.description: Given an integer array nums, return true if any value appears at least twice in the array, and return false if every element is distinct.

examples.explanation: The value 1 appears at index 0 and index 3, so the array contains a duplicate.
All elements are distinct; no value appears more than once.
Several values repeat (for example 1 and 3); we only need to find one duplicate to return true.

learning.keyInsight: Membership tests in a hash set turn duplicate detection from O(n²) scanning into a single O(1) lookup per element.
learning.whyItMatters: Set-based membership is one of the most reused primitives in backend engineering—dedup keys, idempotency checks, and join hash tables all share the same pattern.
learning.lore: The problem of finding duplicates is a fundamental algorithm taught early in computer science, serving as a gateway to understanding time-space tradeoffs. The shift from O(n^2) nested loops to O(n) hash maps is a right of passage for software engineers.

productionFit.title: Idempotency and Deduplication at Scale
productionFit.explanation: In distributed systems, processing the same event twice can cause critical errors (like double-charging a customer). Systems often use distributed caches (like Redis) or Bloom filters to quickly check 'have I seen this ID before?'—which is exactly the Contains Duplicate pattern scaled up.

scaleUp.solution: Partition by hash shard, use external stores (Redis SET, DynamoDB conditional writes), or probabilistic structures (Bloom/HyperLogLog) when exact dedup is too expensive.

applications: Hash joins and GroupBy aggregates in SQL query engines use hash tables to bucket rows by key
Stream deduplication in Kafka/Flink pipelines drops replayed or retried events
In-memory duplicate detection before batch writes prevents unique-constraint violations at the database
hints: Brute force compares every pair of indices—correct but slow for large n.
If you sort first, equal neighbors must be adjacent—what does that simplify?
A hash set answers 'seen before?' in average O(1); walk the array once.

approaches.label: Brute force (all pairs)
approaches.summary: Compare every pair of elements; return true on the first equal pair.
approaches.intuition: Two nested loops exhaustively check whether any two positions hold the same value.
algorithm_steps: Initialize result to false.
For each index i from 0 to n - 2.
For each index j from i + 1 to n - 1.
If nums[i] equals nums[j], return true immediately.
If no pair matched after all loops, return false.

time.explanation: Roughly n(n-1)/2 comparisons in the worst case.
time.best_case: O(1) when the first two elements match
time.worst_case: O(n²) when all elements are distinct

space.explanation: Only loop indices; no auxiliary structure.

steps: i=0 (val=1): compare with j=1 (val=2) -> no match
i=0 (val=1): compare with j=2 (val=3) -> no match
i=0 (val=1): compare with j=3 (val=1) -> MATCH! Return true.

approaches.label: Sort then scan neighbors
approaches.summary: Sort the array; any duplicate appears as two equal adjacent elements.
approaches.intuition: Ordering groups equal values together, so one linear scan after sort suffices.
algorithm_steps: Copy or sort nums in place (note: mutates input if in-place).
Sort the array in ascending order.
Walk indices 1 through n - 1.
Compare nums[i] with nums[i - 1].
If equal, return true; otherwise continue.
Return false if the scan finishes without a match.

space.explanation: O(1) extra if in-place sort allowed; O(n) if copying first.

cons: Mutates input if sorted in place
O(n log n) slower than linear hash scan

steps: i=1: compare nums[1] (1) with nums[0] (1) -> MATCH! Return true.

approaches.label: Hash set membership
approaches.summary: Track seen values in a set; return true the moment a value is inserted twice.
approaches.intuition: Each element asks one question: 'Am I already in the set?' If yes, we found a duplicate; if no, record me and continue.
algorithm_steps: Create an empty hash set seen.
For each value x in nums (left to right).
If x is already in seen, return true immediately.
Otherwise insert x into seen.
After processing all elements without a collision, return false.
Average per-step cost is O(1) thanks to hashing.

time.explanation: Single pass with O(1) average insert/lookup per element.
time.worst_case: O(n) when all distinct (still one pass)

space.explanation: Up to n distinct keys stored before we can prove uniqueness.

steps: x=1: already in seen → return true

ascii_frames:
Pass 2: x=1 → HIT in seen={1,2,3}
       duplicate found → return true

   idx:  0  1  2  3
   val:  1  2  3  1
              ↑────── collision at index 3

approaches.label: Set size vs array length
approaches.summary: Build a set of all elements; duplicates exist iff set size is smaller than array length.
approaches.intuition: A set collapses duplicates automatically—if anything repeated, the set shrinks relative to n.
algorithm_steps: Insert every element of nums into a hash set.
Count distinct elements as set size.
Compare len(set) to len(nums).
If set size < array length, at least one duplicate existed.
Return true when sizes differ, false when equal.

time.explanation: One pass to build the set.

space.explanation: Stores up to n unique keys.

variations.title: Contains Duplicate II
variations.oneLiner: Return true if duplicates are within k indices of each other.

variations.title: Contains Duplicate III
variations.oneLiner: Return true if any two distinct indices differ by at most k and values differ by at most t.

conceptualQuiz.question: Why does the hash-set approach achieve O(n) average time?
options: Because Python sets are always sorted
Because insert and lookup are O(1) average, and we perform one of each per element
Because hashing removes duplicates automatically in one pass without storage
Because we only store half the elements
conceptualQuiz.explanation: Each of n elements triggers at most one average O(1) lookup and one O(1) insert, giving O(n) overall. Sorting would be O(n log n); brute force is O(n²).

debuggingChallenge.bugLocation: The loop always adds every element before checking length; logic is correct but early exit is missing—worse, this version never returns True early when duplicate appears mid-array (still correct answer but the bug is using add without checking membership first, missing the intended early-return pattern). More precisely: swapping add-only for 'if x in seen' loses early termination; for infinite streams it would be wrong.
